extracted.intended_audience: educated British readers of The Spectator — especially clergy, preachers, poets, and essayists (early-18th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance and evaluative principles for composing sermons, sacred music/text pairing, petitions, and descriptive poetry — emphasizing moving the affections, modesty in musical worship, persuasive particulars in petitions, and elevated diction for the sublime. Primarily aimed at clergy, orators, and literary writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacred music should be modest and preparatory
rubrics_metrics.description: A Voluntary before the first Lesson prepares worshippers; the modesty observed in the musical part of our devotions is laudable and preferable to pompous foreign styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music in worship should 'be supposed to prepare' the congregation for reception of divine truths, calming tumults and calming the spirit; prefer modest voluntary and restrained musical expression rather than ostentation that appeals only to the senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music and text must match to move affections appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublime poetry softened in moving strains can humble or exalt the soul; musical expression should be fitted to the sentiment — terrors expressed in music awe into veneration, kind attributes in melody soften into love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rising and sinking of musical lines to reflect and amplify the affections; anthems can relieve and refresh tired spirits between petitions; choose musical treatment that deepens, rather than distracts from, the doctrine being preached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid musical pomp that merely affects the senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Pompous kinds of music that most affect the senses (as seen in some foreign churches) are less desirable than the modest, ordered musical worship advocated here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge church music by its spiritual utility (does it prepare, humble, exalt?) rather than by spectacle or sensory display.

rubrics_metrics.name: True eloquence moves the affections via higher motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian oratory has greater power because it brings consideration of another life, higher rewards and punishments, and thus supplies stronger motives to move the audience's affections than mere temporal arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing sermons or persuasive speech, ground amplification and appeal in doctrines or themes that provide moral weight and eternal consequence (e.g., immortality, resurrection, judgment) to increase persuasive force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue the sublime by enlarging the mind with great subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Study and contemplation of great and glorious mysteries (heavenly bodies, revelation, the mysteries of incarnation) enlarge the mind and enable the orator/poet to reach the marvellous or sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate knowledge of elevated subjects so your imagination and amplification can attain nobility; the sublime is the master-piece of eloquence and requires a mind stretched by lofty objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use amplification and the marvelous as rhetorical mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'marvellous or sublime' is the master-piece of eloquence; amplification drawn from noble subjects gives discourse a noble vigour and invincible force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ amplification (gradations, vivid imagery, elevation of subject) carefully to produce grandeur; the content that most readily yields the sublime is that which touches on eternity, divine mysteries, or large moral consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt rhetorical form to audience and legal/contextual constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Orators must fit their mode to the occasion: where law or custom forbids appeals to the affections (e.g., certain courts), confine yourself to strict argument; in other settings, the stirring of affections is permissible and desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the institutional and cultural constraints of your audience (laws of the forum, expectations of congregation) and choose argumentation vs. affective appeal accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emulate exemplary models (St. Paul) for preaching and eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: St. Paul's harangues and use of revelation are presented as the best examples for clergy to follow; his speeches show visible marks of eloquence and capacity to move diverse audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study exemplary texts (e.g., St. Paul's speeches, Longinus on the sublime) to learn methods of amplification, narrative conversion, and affective appeal; model sermons on passages that combine doctrinal weight with passionate delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic description: give common objects uncommon grace via proportion and diction
rubrics_metrics.description: In description, 'give common objects such uncommon grace' — careful proportion, curious symmetry, and well-chosen words make an ordinary subject appear beautiful and wondrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose descriptions with attention to symmetry, arrangement of details, and 'well-chosen words in every line'; meter ('numbers') should warm the lines and diction should temper imagery so the description charms as the object does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match poetic method to effect: proportion, symmetry, and harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful decorative or descriptive poem arranges parts (pebbles, shells, colours) in 'curious symmetry' so art imparts more beauty than chance; similarly, poetic lines should be proportioned and harmoniously ordered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structural ordering (formal symmetry, careful placement of details, harmonic phrasing) to produce the sense that art gives 'more than Nature gave' — let craft illuminate and enhance the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitions should present genuine, meritorious, and relevant sufferings/services
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims for patronage or office should rest on suffered services that promoted a good cause and were undeserved; sufferings arising from rashness or follies do not merit recompense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting petitions: include concrete incidents of service, specific harms endured that contributed to the cause, demonstrate relevance to the requested office, and end with a humble formula of request; avoid absurd or whimsical claims (e.g., 'roasted an ox' as sole merit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain decorum in sacred contexts and avoid provoking ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter in places where things sacred are transacted is far less pardonable than levity elsewhere; novelty or sublime language that surpasses the congregation's comprehension can provoke ridicule and defeat the sermon’s purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing and delivering sermons, keep order and decency in view; pitch novelty and elevation to the audience's capacity, and avoid unnecessary ostentation that draws ridicule rather than reverence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleanliness signals politeness and refines sentiment (social-virtue guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleanliness is a mark of politeness, fosters love, preserves health, and bears analogy to purity of mind; outward neatness suggests inward refined sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In portraying characters or advising comportment, use cleanliness as a social signifier of civility and moral disposition; emphasize habitual neatness to imply steadiness of thought and refined passions.
